A half-day hike · Mount Tamalpais, Marin County, California

The balcony of Mount Tam

A loop along the sunny south face of the mountain, high above the fog: out on a contour path with San Francisco at your feet, lemonade on the porch of a 1904 railway inn, and home through cool forest.

7.6 km4.7 miles, loop
≈ 250 mtotal climb & descent
2½–3 hwith a stop at the inn
600 → 415 mstart → lowest point
Easy–moderateone real climb, at the end

Why this walk

This is the mountain’s greatest-hits loop, and the easiest way to understand why people who live here never leave. You start at 600 m, already above most of the Bay Area, so the views begin in the car park and do not stop for an hour.

  • The view. The outward leg is a balcony: the Pacific on your right, the city straight ahead, the bay and Mount Diablo to the left, often with a white sea of fog filling everything below you.
  • Five landscapes in two hours. Windy meadow, bare green rock, scented scrub, oak woodland, redwood ravines. They change every few hundred metres, and page 4 explains why.
  • Two good stories. A stone amphitheatre built by hand in the 1930s, and the last surviving building of “the crookedest railroad in the world”.
  • A proper stop. The West Point Inn’s porch is the best-placed bench in Marin.

Is this for me?

Easier than the Muir Woods loop: shorter, with less climbing. If you can walk briskly for two hours you can do this.

Overall effortLike a brisk 10 km walk on the flat. About two hours of walking.
The shapeIt is an “upside-down” hike: you start at the top, lose height gently for 6 km, and pay it all back in the last 1.2 km.
The climb170 m up at an average 14%: 25–30 minutes of steady uphill, about two Dom Towers of stairs, in shade. Then it is over.
UnderfootNarrow dirt paths, rocky in places on the first half; one short steep descent (Nora Trail). Shoes with grip.
SunThe first 3 km are fully exposed. Hat, sunscreen and water even on a cool day.

What you can see, and where

Rock Spring car parkWest over the grassy ridge to the Pacific. On a clear day the Farallon Islands sit on the horizon, 45 km out to sea.
Mountain Theater, top rowSouth-east over the stage: Richardson Bay, the Tiburon peninsula, Angel Island, the Bay Bridge and the East Bay hills, with Mount Diablo (1,173 m) behind.
Rock Spring TrailThe whole south face opens up. San Francisco’s towers above the Marin Headlands, with a tower of the Golden Gate Bridge showing over the ridge; below you the dark, forested canyon that holds Muir Woods; to the right the open ocean.
West Point Inn porchThe same panorama, sitting down. Look back up and left for the fire lookout on East Peak (784 m), the summit.
Matt Davis TrailMostly in forest, with windows: each time the path rounds an open spur you get the city and bay again, framed by trees.

In summer, fog often fills the bay to 300–500 m, and from this trail you look down on it: only bridge towers, the tallest buildings and hilltops stand clear.

Step by step

DistanceWhat to do, and what to look for
10.0 km603 m Rock Spring car park, where Pantoll Road meets Ridgecrest Boulevard. Cross the road and take the signed path to the Mountain Theater, through open meadow and scattered oaks.
20.5 km · 0.3 mi619 m — high point The Mountain Theater (officially the Cushing Memorial Amphitheatre). Walk in and sit down for a minute: curving rows of stone, each block set by hand by the young men of the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, seating nearly 4,000. The Mountain Play has been staged here most springs since 1913; the audience once came by train and on foot. Water and toilets. The signed Rock Spring Trail to West Point Inn leaves from the upper edge of the theatre.
0.5–2.9 kmgently downhill The balcony. The Rock Spring Trail contours east for 2.4 km, losing only 70 m. It crosses patches of bare, greenish rock (serpentine, see page 4), then long open slopes of chaparral, dipping into small shady ravines of oak and bay. The views are continuous; so is the sun. The path is narrow and stony: admire the view standing still.
32.9 km · 1.8 mi549 m West Point Inn. The trail drops onto a wide dirt road, the Old Railroad Grade, at the inn. Take a break on the porch (see box). To continue, find the signed Nora Trail, leaving downhill from the front of the inn below the picnic tables. It descends steeply on switchbacks, quickly leaving the sun for forest.
43.8 km · 2.4 mi417 m — low point The Nora Trail ends at the Matt Davis Trail. Turn right (west), signed for Bootjack and Pantoll. The next 2 km mirror the outward leg: the same mountainside 150 m lower, mostly in forest. The trail rolls in and out of ravines, each with its stream, ferns and a few redwoods, and between them rounds drier spurs with madrone, manzanita and sudden views. Matt Davis, who built it in the 1920s, was the dean of the mountain’s trail builders; note how evenly it is graded.
55.8 km · 3.6 mi434 m Bootjack. Just above the Bootjack picnic area and the highway, the Matt Davis Trail meets the Bootjack Trail. Turn right, uphill, signed for the Mountain Theater. This is the climb: 170 m in 1.2 km on a well-built path with steps, through forest, straight across the Old Stage Road (a wide dirt road) and up to the theatre. Take it steadily; it is 25–30 minutes.
27.1 km · 4.4 mi602 m You emerge beside the Mountain Theater again. Retrace the first ten minutes back across the meadow to the road.
17.6 km · 4.7 mi603 m Back at Rock Spring. With energy and light to spare, O’Rourke’s Bench, ten minutes west on a signed path, is the classic sunset seat.

The West Point Inn

From 1896 to 1930 a steam railway climbed Mount Tamalpais from Mill Valley, through 281 curves in 13 km: “the crookedest railroad in the world”. This was its westernmost point, where a stagecoach met the train to carry passengers down to Stinson Beach and Bolinas. The inn was built for them in 1904. The Old Stage Road you cross on the way home was the coach road; the Old Railroad Grade outside the door is the trackbed.

The inn survives, run by volunteers, with no mains electricity and no public road. The porch, picnic tables, toilets and drinking water are open to walkers by day, and simple drinks and snacks are often on sale: bring a little cash, but do not rely on it. You can stay the night, by reservation at westpointinn.com.

Field notes

Five worlds in seven kilometres — and why

On this loop the landscape changes like a slideshow: grass, bare rock, scrub, woodland, redwoods, sometimes within a hundred paces. None of it is random. Four things decide what grows on any given square metre of this mountain: how much summer sun it gets, whether the fog reaches it, what rock lies underneath, and when it last burned.

The setting: a Mediterranean climate with a cold ocean

California’s coast has the same climate type as Spain: mild wet winters, and summers with no rain at all from May to October. Every plant here has to solve the same problem you know from the hills around Madrid: six months of drought. The difference is the sea. The California Current brings cold water down the coast, and in summer warm inland air drawn across it condenses into a bank of fog that pours through the Golden Gate most afternoons and sits against the mountain up to roughly 300–500 m. This trail runs along the top of that fog line, which is why the vegetation is so mixed: you are walking the border between the fog-watered world below and the sun-baked one above.

1 · Ridge-top grasslandRock Spring, km 0–0.5
Open meadow, golden from June, green from December, full of wildflowers in April. Wind, thin soil and summer drought keep trees out, but so did people: for thousands of years the Coast Miwok burned these ridges to keep them open for game and seed plants, and ranchers then grazed them. Without either, Douglas fir is slowly moving in; look for young firs standing alone in the grass.
2 · Serpentine barrensaround the Theater and the first part of the Rock Spring Trail
The slick blue-green rock is serpentine, a piece of the Earth’s mantle scraped up at the plate boundary. It makes terrible soil: almost no calcium, nitrogen or phosphorus, and toxic levels of magnesium, nickel and chromium. Most plants cannot live on it, so it looks half-bare. Those that can are specialists found almost nowhere else: the stunted, grey-green Sargent cypress, leather oak, and a manzanita that grows only on this mountain. Where the rock changes, the plants change along a line you could draw with a ruler.
3 · ChaparralRock Spring Trail, the open south-facing slopes
Dense, head-high evergreen scrub: manzanita (smooth mahogany bark), chamise, ceanothus and scrub oak. It is the Californian twin of the Spanish matorral and the French maquis, evolved separately for the same climate; even the name is Spanish, from chaparro, a scrub oak. South-facing slopes take the sun square-on all summer, so plants here have small, thick, waxy leaves, often held edge-on to the light, to lose as little water as possible. Chaparral is built to burn: every few decades fire clears it, and it regrows from buried root crowns and from seeds that germinate only after heat or smoke. A fire in 1929 swept much of this face.
4 · Mixed evergreen woodlandevery ravine, and most of the Matt Davis Trail
Step round a corner onto a north- or east-facing fold and you are in shade: coast live oak, California bay laurel (crush a leaf: peppery, like strong bay), tanoak, Douglas fir, and madrone, with peeling orange bark. Madrid will recognise that one. It is Arbutus menziesii, the big American cousin of the madroño on the city’s coat of arms, and Spanish missionaries named it for the resemblance. These folds get a fraction of the summer sun, hold cool air and keep soil moisture into August. Aspect alone, a few degrees of turn in the hillside, is the whole difference between this and the scrub fifty metres away.
5 · Redwood ravinescreek crossings on the Nora, Matt Davis and Bootjack trails
Coast redwoods, the tallest trees on Earth, need more water than the rain here provides, and they get it from the air. Their needles comb droplets out of the summer fog, which drip to the ground and can add a third or more to the year’s water. So redwoods grow only where the fog reaches and the soil is deep: on this loop that means the stream gullies, near the upper limit of their range. The giants are 300 m below you in Muir Woods; up here they are slimmer, and each grove marks a place where fog and water collect.

Who lives here. Turkey vultures and red-tailed hawks ride the updraughts along the south face at eye level. Western fence lizards do push-ups on the trail-side rocks. In the forest listen for the harsh call of the Steller’s jay (dark blue, crested), and after rain look for banana slugs, bright yellow and as long as your hand. Deer are common at dusk in the meadows.

Getting to Rock Spring

Driving route from the Golden Gate Bridge: 26 km (16 miles). Basemap: USGS The National Map. Route: OpenStreetMap via OSRM.

Parking and gates

Rock Spring has a free car park with toilets; no reservation. It fills by mid-morning on fine weekends; there is more roadside parking along Ridgecrest Boulevard. The road gates are locked at sunset (the park is open 7:00 to sunset): be back at the car with time to spare.

Roadworks, November 2026: Pantoll Road is being resurfaced on weekdays until about 20 November, with one-way traffic control. Allow extra time on a weekday.

Rock Spring trailhead, junction of Pantoll Road and Ridgecrest Boulevard, Mount Tamalpais State Park. Allow 40 minutes from the Golden Gate Bridge, 55 from central San Francisco.

ACross the Golden Gate Bridge northbound on US 101.
B9 km (5½ mi) from the start of the bridge, take the exit signed Highway 1 / Stinson Beach / Mill Valley.
CAfter 1.6 km (1 mi), at the lights at Tam Junction, turn left to stay on Highway 1.
DAfter 4.2 km (2.6 mi) turn right onto Panoramic Highway, signed Mount Tamalpais.
EAt the four-way junction after 1.6 km (1 mi) keep straight on, the upper road. You pass the Mountain Home Inn, then Bootjack.
F8.6 km (5.3 mi) after joining Panoramic Highway, at Pantoll ranger station, turn right onto Pantoll Road, signed for the Mountain Theater and East Peak.
P2.3 km (1.4 mi) uphill, where Pantoll Road meets Ridgecrest Boulevard, the Rock Spring car park is directly ahead.

Without a car, or if Rock Spring is full

Marin Transit route 61 stops at Pantoll, ten minutes’ walk along the Matt Davis Trail from point 5. Start the loop there and walk it in the same direction, with the climb first and the inn two-thirds of the way round. Drivers can do the same from the Bootjack or Pantoll car parks (parking fee).

Practical

  • Water: taps at the Mountain Theater and the West Point Inn. Carry a litre each anyway.
  • Sun and wind: the first half has no shade and the ridge is often windy; the forest half can be 8 °C cooler. Bring a hat and a layer.
  • When: all year. April–May for wildflowers and green hills; summer for the sea of fog; autumn for the clearest air; winter after rain for running creeks (and mud on the Nora Trail).
  • Daylight: in winter the sun sets around 17:00. Start by 13:00 at the latest.
  • Poison oak (glossy leaves in threes, red in autumn) lines the forest sections; do not touch. Check for ticks afterwards. Rattlesnakes sun themselves on the rocky first half in warm weather: watch your feet, and give one room.
  • No dogs or bikes on these trails. Leave nothing visible in the car. Emergency: 911; rangers +1 415 388 2070.

Afterwards

On the way down: the Mountain Home Inn is 5 km back along Panoramic Highway, with a deck over the bay. Casual food; check opening hours first (+1 415 381 9000).

In Mill Valley, 20 minutes down the hill (left at the four-way junction, E):

  • Playa — modern Mexican, patio, good margaritas. Closed Monday.
  • Sol Food — Puerto Rican, counter service, open all afternoon: the hungry hiker’s choice.
  • Bungalow 44 — lively Californian dinner and cocktails.
  • Buckeye Roadhouse — the classic 1937 roadhouse by the Highway 101 junction; book ahead.

Kitchens close around 21:00, early by Madrid standards. Hours change: check on the day.
